title: Count Set Bits
statement:
Count how many bits are set in a 32-bit unsigned value.

## Your procedure

```
int count_set_bits(unsigned int value);
```

`count_set_bits(0)` is `0`, `count_set_bits(7)` is `3`, and
`count_set_bits(0xFFFFFFFF)` is `32`.

## The calling convention

Microsoft x64. The first four integer or pointer arguments arrive in
registers, and a 32-bit result goes back in `eax`:

| | 1st | 2nd | 3rd | 4th | return |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 64-bit | `rcx` | `rdx` | `r8` | `r9` | `rax` |
| 32-bit | `ecx` | `edx` | `r8d` | `r9d` | `eax` |

`rax`, `rcx`, `rdx`, `r8`-`r11` are yours to clobber. `rbx`, `rbp`, `rsi`,
`rdi` and `r12`-`r15` belong to the caller: use one and you must `push` it on
the way in and `pop` it on the way out.

Nothing here needs the stack, so nothing here needs a prologue.

## Watch out

- `popcnt` does the whole job in one instruction. It passes these tests and
  misses the point of the exercise -- shift the bits out yourself.
- The value is **unsigned**, so shift it right with `shr`, never `sar`.
  `sar` copies the sign bit down, and a value with the top bit set would
  then never reach zero: the loop would run forever and the case would come
  back `TIMEOUT` rather than with a wrong answer.
- `shr` puts the bit it shifted out into the carry flag, which `jc` and `jnc`
  can branch on -- one way to do this, though testing the low bit with `and`
  works just as well.
starter_code:
; int count_set_bits(unsigned int value)
;
;   ecx = value (the bits to count)
;   eax = how many of them are set

.code
count_set_bits PROC
    ; your code here
    xor eax, eax
    ret
count_set_bits ENDP
end

tests.name: zero
tests.description: The loop must not run at all.

tests.name: all ones
tests.description: The top bit is set. With `sar` instead of `shr` this case never terminates.

tests.name: top bit only
tests.description: One set bit, but it takes 32 shifts to reach it.
